newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul stocks seen moderately higher on yen rally.
newsitem.headline: Seoul stocks seen moderately higher on yen rally.

text.p: The continued strength of the Japanese yen against the dollar was seen pulling South Korean share prices moderately higher on Friday following two days of sharp increases, traders said.

"Investors are clearly favoring stocks that they see benefitting from the strong yen," said Alex Kim, trader at H.G. Asia. "Many are now thinking that the economy may hit bottom and begin a turnaround."
The Korea composite price index rose 2.35 percent or 16.09 points to 699.95 on Thursday. That followed Tuesday's sharp rise of 1.75 percent. Wednesday was a market holiday.
The index briefly broke through the psychological barrier of 700 in early Thursday afternoon trading before falling back.
More than 51 million shares worth 742 billion won changed hands, and advancing shares swamped decliners by 544 to 252.
Kim said the index would begin the morning session on Friday moving higher. Profit-taking in the afternoon could bring it lower, but it should still end in positive territory, he said.

The continued strength of the Japanese yen provided a strong lift to core Korean blue chips. The prevailing belief is that a strong yen would make Korean goods from autos to steel products more competitive in overseas markets.
The yen was trading at 116.20/22 against the dollar in late trading on Thursday in Tokyo. The yen stood at 115.75/85 in New York trading late on Thursday.
Traders said large-cap, low-priced shares have attracted strong interest.
Shares in five of the Daewoo Group's nine listed firms went limit-up on Thursday, including Daewoo Heavy Industries, Daewoo Electronics, Daewoo Telecom, Daewoo Securities and Daewoo Corp.
Also up sharply were Samsung Electronics, LG Electronics, Pohang Iron and Steel, Hyundai Motor and Yukong.
The market shrugged off news of the bankruptcy of Korea's largest confectionery maker, Samlip General Foods Co Trading of the stock was suspended from Thursday morning.

Investors also paid no attention to the scandal surrounding presidential son Kim Hyun-chul, who was questioned by prosecutors on Thursday afternoon. He is suspected of taking kickbacks and peddling influence. His arrest is expected soon but traders said the market had already absorbed the news.
